title: Testing
note: Tests are an executable record of what the code should do. Unit tests check small pieces in isolation, integration tests check that pieces work together, and end-to-end tests drive the whole system. The test pyramid says to write many fast unit tests and progressively fewer slow, broad ones.

read.title: What tests can and cannot tell you
text: A unit test runs in milliseconds and points straight at the broken function. An end-to-end test clicks through the real application and catches problems no unit test can see, such as two services disagreeing about a date format, but it is slow and breaks when the UI shifts. The test pyramid balances these costs: a wide base of unit tests, a middle layer of integration tests, and a thin top of end-to-end tests.

To isolate a unit, tests replace its dependencies with test doubles. A stub returns canned answers. A mock also checks that it was called in the expected way. A fake is a real but lightweight implementation, such as an in-memory database. Overusing mocks ties tests to implementation details, so a harmless refactor can break dozens of them.

Coverage tools report which lines or branches the tests executed. That is useful for finding untested code, but a line can run without any assertion checking its result. As Dijkstra observed, testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence. Mutation testing gives a sharper signal: it deliberately breaks the code in small ways and asks whether any test notices.

q.q: What risk comes with overusing mocks?
